title: The Alphabet of the Magi
otherNames: Alphabet of the Magi: the English name. Wikipedia reports that S. L. MacGregor Mathers used it for this alphabet on Plate XV of his Key of Solomon (preface dated October 1888; title page 1889).
The characters of the angel Raphael: Claude Duret's label in his Thrésor (1613), citing Ambrogio. Reported by Wikipedia and by the Lyon library blog on Duret (bibulyon.hypotheses.org).
Alphabet of the Magi of Paracelsus / 'Paracelsus' alphabet': the modern attribution, e.g. Omniglot ('invented by ... Paracelsus in the 16th century').
Alphabet of Apollonius of Tyana: found only on dCode. No historical source was found, and dCode may not be used for history under the house rule. Do not print it as an attested name.

Alphabet des mages: the caption of a Flickr image (user cenacledelarc, 2010) says the image is an extract from Paul Christian's Histoire de la magie (1870). The image was not seen, so it is unverified whether its letters are this alphabet.
family: A variant of the Hebrew alphabet. Wikipedia describes the earliest printed version (Teseo Ambrogio, Pavia 1539) as variant glyphs labelled Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth and so on through Thau, i.e. keyed to the Hebrew letters in Hebrew order. That rests on Wikipedia; the 1539 print was not viewed. It is NOT one of Agrippa's alphabets (De occulta philosophia III.29–30). It is often charted beside his Celestial, Malachim and Transitus fluvii, but its graphic relation to that ring-letter (Brillenbuchstaben) family is unverified. Its documented route runs through alphabet compendia: Ambrogio 1539, Duret 1613 and Fry 1799. Mathers then printed it under the name 'Alphabet of the Magi' (1888). The Paracelsus attribution is later than all of these, and no source cites a passage for it.
summary: The 'Alphabet of the Magi' is a variant of the Hebrew alphabet. Its earliest known printing is in Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi's Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam (Pavia, 1539). According to Wikipedia (the 1539 print was not viewed), Ambrogio says the letters were held to have been invented by Gamaliel and handed down in a book called Liber ignis, associated with the angel Raphiel. Claude Duret reprinted it in 1613 as 'the characters of the angel Raphael', Edmund Fry in his Pantographia (1799), and S. L. MacGregor Mathers on Plate XV of his Key of Solomon (1888) under the name 'Alphabet of the Magi'. Modern reference charts credit it to Paracelsus and say he engraved angels' names with it on healing and protective talismans, but no source found cites a passage of Paracelsus for this.

firstAttestation.work: Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam, Syriacam, atque Armenicam, & decem alias linguas. Characterum differentium alphabeta, circiter quadraginta, & eorundem inuicem conformatio. Mystica et cabalistica quamplurima scitu digna. Et descriptio ac simulachrum Phagoti Afranij. Title as given in the WorldCat (OCLC 954792662) and Library of Congress (09016522) records.
firstAttestation.author: Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi (Theseus Ambrosius ex comitibus Albonesii). Dates 1469–1540 per the Library of Congress heading and Wikipedia; the ADER (Paris) auction catalogue gives c. 1469–c. 1540.
firstAttestation.date: 1539 (LOC, WorldCat, ADER). ADER reports that the first edition exists in two issues, with March and April calendar dates in the colophon. It does not say whether the alphabet differs between them.
firstAttestation.place: Pavia: Giovanni Maria Simonetta (ADER auction catalogue).
firstAttestation.locator: Two readings, unresolved. Wikipedia ('Alphabet of the Magi') cites 'pp. 202f.', not checked against a scan. But the book is foliated, not paginated (ADER: 215 ff. plus 1 blank), and Wikipedia's article on Ambrogio puts the appendix of alphabets at fols. 193–213. The reference is therefore probably to fol. 202 and the following leaf, with recto/verso not established. Confirm on the Internet Archive scan (bub_gb_yUkKq_QnrnwC) or the Library of Congress copy before the page prints a locator.
firstAttestation.notes: This replaces the research file's candidate, Paul Christian's Histoire de la magie (1870). That candidate is refuted: the alphabet was printed at least three times before 1870 (Ambrogio 1539, Duret 1613, Fry 1799). BASIS: Wikipedia's 'Alphabet of the Magi', which names the work and the page. Three other sources agree. dCode says the first known publication was Ambrosius's in 1539; it is listed only as agreeing, since the house rule bars it for history. Wikipedia quotes Fry, who reports Ambrosius's account. The Lyon library blog on Duret (bibulyon.hypotheses.org) says Duret's 'alphabet of the Angel Raphael' is taken from Theseus Ambrosius. The primary print was NOT viewed: there is no page fetching, and images cannot be downloaded. TWO CAUTIONS from the ADER description. (1) The book prints some of its c. 38–40 alphabets and leaves spaces in which others were added by hand in ink, so a given copy's forms may be hand-drawn and may differ from copy to copy. (2) There are two issues. AN EARLIER PRINTING IS NOT EXCLUDED. The same Flickr caption says Christian's 'alphabet des mages' also appears 'with many others' in Pantheus's Voarchadumia. Wikipedia's Transitus Fluvii article dates that book to Venice, 1530, but its bibliography cites a 1550 copy. If the Voarchadumia alphabet is this one, the first attestation moves to 1530. Unverified.

transmission.work: Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam, Syriacam, atque Armenicam, & decem alias linguas (Pavia: G. M. Simonetta)
transmission.author: Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi (Theseus Ambrosius)
transmission.what: Earliest known printing. Ambrogio gives the alphabet among about forty alphabets, in an appendix at fols. 193–213 (per Wikipedia's Ambrogio article), as variant Hebrew glyphs labelled Aleph to Thau. Per Wikipedia, it differs from his other Semitic variants because he reports that these letters were said to have been invented by Gamaliel and handed down in a book called Liber ignis associated with the angel Raphiel; Wikipedia tags that sentence 'clarification needed'. The primary print was not viewed.

transmission.author: Paracelsus, ed. Johannes Huser
transmission.what: First collected edition of the writings under Paracelsus' name. The dates come from the house timeline, which is not an independent source. Joseph H. Peterson's Esoteric Archives edition of the Archidoxis magica states that the text first appeared in 1591, in Huser's collected works. Wikipedia asserts that this alphabet 'is described' in the Archidoxis magica, but gives no page and is tagged 'page needed'. No such passage was found.

transmission.work: Thrésor de l'histoire des langues de cest univers (Cologny: M. Berjon; USTC 1700883)
transmission.author: Claude Duret (1570?–1611), published posthumously
transmission.what: Reprints the alphabet as 'the characters of the angel Raphael', citing Ambrogio (Wikipedia). The Lyon library blog on Duret (bibulyon.hypotheses.org) says Duret reproduces an alphabet of the Angel Raphael taken from Theseus Ambrosius, without taking a position on its authenticity. Imprints vary: USTC gives Cologny; the same blog notes copies with Geneva and Cologny addresses; Open Library names the printer M. Berjon. The page is DISPUTED: Wikipedia says p. 117, but its own Google Books link points to p. 125 (PA125).

transmission.work: Of the Supreme Mysteries of Nature (includes the Archidoxes of Magic), London: N. Brook and J. Harison
transmission.author: Paracelsus (attributed), tr. Robert Turner
transmission.what: English route for the pseudo-Paracelsian Archidoxis magica, whose zodiacal and planetary seals carry names and characters. The imprint comes from a search result describing Turner's edition. A Wellcome Collection record describes a 1975 reprint; the publisher (Askin) and Stephen Skinner's introduction rest on prior knowledge. Wikipedia names Turner's translation as the English route for the alphabet, but gives no page ('page needed'), and this check found no passage.

transmission.author: Edmund Fry
transmission.what: Reproduces the alphabet, pp. 28–29 according to Wikipedia. PARAPHRASE (not a quotation; the wording seen is Wikipedia's transcription and was not checked against the 1799 print): Fry reports Ambrosius's assertion that the angel Raphael brought this character from heaven and gave it to Adam, who used it to compose psalms after his expulsion from the earthly paradise. This Raphael-and-Adam story differs from the Gamaliel and Liber ignis account that Wikipedia gives for Ambrogio himself; both are reported versions. The heading under which Fry prints it was not confirmed.

transmission.work: Histoire de la magie, du monde surnaturel et de la fatalité à travers les temps et les peuples (Paris: Furne, Jouvet et Cie)
transmission.author: P. Christian (Jean-Baptiste Pitois, 1811–1877)
transmission.what: NOT the first printing (see 1539, 1613, 1799). The imprint and date are confirmed by dealer listings (livre-rare-book, AbeBooks) and the Gallica record, and Pitois's dates by Wikipedia. Dealers describe 16 woodcut plates; another listing gives 15. A Flickr image captioned 'Alphabet des mages' is described by its uploader as an extract from this book. The image was not seen, so neither its plate or page nor its identity with this alphabet is verified.

transmission.work: The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis), Plate XV, 'The Mystical Alphabets'
transmission.author: S. Liddell MacGregor Mathers (ed., tr.)
transmission.what: Prints the alphabet on Plate XV under the name 'Alphabet of the Magi' (Wikipedia). The plate's title, 'The Mystical Alphabets', is from the sacred-texts.com table of contents. This is the earliest use of the English name found in this check; whether Mathers coined it is not established. The publisher (George Redway) rests on prior knowledge.

Search snippets show that it states the alphabet was 'invented by Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (also known as Paracelsus) in the 16th century' and that 'He used it to engrave the names of angels on talismans'. claims.claim: Paracelsus devised the Alphabet of the Magi.
claims.evidence: Omniglot states that it 'was invented by Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (also known as Paracelsus) in the 16th century' (wording seen in search snippets). No source found cites a work, chapter or folio of Paracelsus for it. The earliest known printing, Ambrogio 1539, appeared two years before Paracelsus' death. As reported, it gives a different pedigree (Gamaliel, Liber ignis, the angel Raphiel) and does not name Paracelsus. Wikipedia and the Voynich wiki treat the attribution as later. The page should write 'attributed to Paracelsus in modern reference works; no passage in his writings has been identified'.

claims.claim: The alphabet is found in Paracelsus' Archidoxis magica.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia asserts that the alphabet 'is described in the pseudo-Paracelsian Archidoxis magica, translated into English by R. Turner (1656)', but tags the claim 'page needed'. This check found no passage. Even if it were true, it would not make the alphabet Paracelsus' own, and it could not be the first printing: per Peterson, the Archidoxis magica first appeared in Huser's edition in 1591, and Ambrogio printed the alphabet in 1539. On authenticity, the house timeline's 'spurious by common consent' is stronger than the sources seen. Wikipedia calls the work pseudo-Paracelsian and reports Wolfgang Schneider's 1982 study as finding it spurious, though perhaps partly from Paracelsus' lifetime. Peterson's Esoteric Archives page reportedly says Schneider thought the first four books could be genuine, and raises Jacques Gohory as a possible author. The two reports of Schneider disagree; both are given.

claims.claim: It is not one of the alphabets printed by Agrippa.
claims.evidence: Re-verified in this pass from the EEBO-TCP transcription of the 1651 English (A26565, local clone in the scratchpad). III.29, 'Of the Characters and Seals of spirits', begins on p. 437. Its letters 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes' are on p. 438. III.30, 'Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists', begins on p. 439 and names the Celestial, Malachim and 'the passing through the River'. The word 'Magi' does not occur anywhere in the 1651 text. For 1533, Wikipedia ('Theban alphabet') gives III.29 and Omniglot gives III.30 for the River script. The Library of Congress holds the Cologne 1533 edition (item 20007812), which was not viewed.

claims.claim: It first appears in Paul Christian's Histoire de la magie (Paris, 1870).
claims.evidence: REFUTED as stated. The alphabet is reported in print in 1539 (Ambrogio), 1613 (Duret) and 1799 (Fry), all before 1870. At most, Christian is a later witness. A Flickr caption says an 'Alphabet des mages' image comes from his book, and the same caption says the alphabet is also in Pantheus's Voarchadumia. The image was not seen, and its identity with this alphabet is unverified.

claims.claim: Paul Christian credited his own constructions to ancient authorities.
claims.evidence: The blog 'Egypt in the tarot' quotes Decker, Depaulis and Dummett, who judge Christian's 'Egyptian initiation' to be his invention from start to finish, with not one word matching Iamblichus' On the Mysteries. The blog adds that Christian's footnote cites a specific edition, a 1687 Oxford folio of Iamblichus. The book itself is confirmed as published (London: Duckworth, 1996; WorldCat), but its page was not seen. Since the Christian hypothesis is refuted, this claim no longer bears on the alphabet's origin. It is context only, for the 'alphabet des mages' label.

claims.evidence: Wikipedia says Ambrosius gives variant glyphs of the Hebrew alphabet, labelled Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth and so on to Thau. This rests on Wikipedia; the 1539 print was not viewed. That the set is exactly the 22 non-final letters, with no finals or extra signs, was NOT independently confirmed: only Grokipedia, an unreliable source, states 22.

claims.claim: The alphabet carries the Latin values A, B, G, D, E, U/V, Z, H, Th, I/J/Y, C/K, L, M, N, X, O, F/P, Ts, Q, R, S, T.
claims.evidence: These values are not reported for the 1539 printing, which labels the signs by Hebrew letter names. They are modern conventions. Per a search summary of dCode's table, dCode gives Samekh = X and Tav = T, and warns that no exact Hebrew–Latin correspondence exists. Omniglot's values were not seen. A secondary site that reprints Papus partly confirms that Paul Christian's arcana use similar values: XVII, 'the Star of the Magi', under F/P (80), and XXI, 'the Crown of the Magi', under T (400). That shows a shared 19th-century convention, not an origin. Use the values only as the site's transliteration convention, and label them so.

claims.evidence: This is Ambrogio's reported pedigree for the letters, per Wikipedia, which tags the sentence 'clarification needed'. Report it as 'Ambrogio says these letters were held to have been invented by Gamaliel...', never as fact. Fry's 1799 version is different: Raphael brought them from heaven to Adam. Both versions should be given and attributed.

letters.name: Aleph
letters.form: NOT DESCRIBED. No image of this alphabet was seen, in research or in fact-check, and no text describes its letters stroke by stroke. Do not reconstruct the forms from memory of modern charts or fonts. Do not borrow them from the Celestial, Malachim or Transitus fluvii, or from the Hebrew square letter: no source says how far they are related. The earliest printing is now identified: Teseo Ambrogio, Introductio, Pavia 1539, near fol. (or p.) 202 per Wikipedia. Trace from a scan of that print (Internet Archive bub_gb_yUkKq_QnrnwC; Library of Congress 09016522), compare Duret 1613 and Mathers 1888, Plate XV, and say where they differ. Caution: per the ADER auction description, some of the 1539 alphabets were added by hand in ink, so the forms may vary from copy to copy. Name the copy traced.

The print was not viewed, and the exact count of 22 is not independently confirmed. LATIN VALUE 'A': a modern-chart convention, not in the 1539 source. Use it only as the site's transliteration, and label it so. The research file's tie to Paul Christian's arcana is withdrawn as evidence of origin. NUMERIC 1: the standard Hebrew value, supplied for the transliterator; no source seen prints numbers with this alphabet.

uses.use: A specimen in Renaissance and early-modern alphabet compendia
uses.evidence: Documented: Ambrogio prints it among about forty alphabets (1539), Duret reprints it (1613), and Fry reproduces it (1799). Per Wikipedia and the Lyon library blog; the prints were not viewed.

uses.use: Engraving angel names on talismans (the attributed Paracelsian use)
uses.evidence: Legend. Asserted by Omniglot without a cited source. Wikipedia's lead speaks of talisman inscriptions in 17th-century occultism, and no source for that was checked. The Archidoxis magica prescribes seals with names and characters, but no passage using this alphabet was found.

Mathers includes it on Plate XV, 'The Mystical Alphabets', of his Key of Solomon (1888/1889). Per Wikipedia and the sacred-texts.com table of contents. Whether Mathers' text prescribes it for any pentacle was not checked.

Modern web charts and free fonts circulate it as a 'magical alphabet' for writing names (Omniglot links free fonts, per search snippets). This shows modern circulation only; it is not evidence of historical use.

links.relation: In its earliest printing (Ambrogio 1539, per Wikipedia) the signs are variant glyphs labelled with the Hebrew letter names in Hebrew order, Aleph to Thau.
Modern charts add Latin values (A, B, G, D, E, U/V, Z, H, Th, I/J/Y, C/K, L, M, N, X, O, F/P, Ts, Q, R, S, T). These are later conventions, not in the 1539 print.
Often charted beside it. Malachim is Agrippa's (1651 English III.30, p. 439, verified); the Alphabet of the Magi is not. Any graphic relation is unverified.

Often shown in the same 'magical alphabets' charts as the Celestial, which Agrippa prints (1651 III.30, p. 439, verified). The Alphabet of the Magi is not Agrippa's; it comes by a separate route (Ambrogio 1539, Duret 1613).

Listed in the same modern charts. Both have Renaissance printings, by separate routes. Transitus fluvii: Wikipedia gives de Balmes, Peculium Abrae, Venice 1523, sig. B6v, and Agrippa III.30. The Alphabet of the Magi: Ambrogio 1539 and Duret 1613.

Both alphabets come with attributions, reported as such. Theban: Agrippa gives the letters 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes' (1651 III.29, p. 438, verified), and Wikipedia says Trithemius' Polygraphia (1518) attributes it to Honorius of Thebes. Alphabet of the Magi: Ambrogio reports a Gamaliel and Liber ignis pedigree, and modern charts ascribe it to Paracelsus.

cautions: This fact-check ran WebSearch only: no page fetching, and no images. The search budget ran out before every point could be closed (see unresolved). The 1539, 1613 and 1799 prints were NOT viewed; their contents and locators rest on Wikipedia, corroborated where stated.

Never write 'Paracelsus invented / devised the Alphabet of the Magi'. Write 'modern reference works attribute it to Paracelsus; it is printed in 1539 by Teseo Ambrogio, who gives it a different pedigree, and no passage in Paracelsus' writings has been identified'.
Do not name Paul Christian (1870) as the first printing. That candidate is refuted by printings in 1539, 1613 and 1799.

Report Ambrogio's pedigree as his report: the letters were held to have been invented by Gamaliel and handed down in a Liber ignis associated with the angel Raphiel. Report Fry's Raphael-to-Adam story as Fry's report of Ambrogio. Neither is fact, and the two versions differ.
Locators are not settled: Ambrogio 'pp. 202f.' (Wikipedia) against a foliated book (fols. 193–213 for the alphabets); Duret p. 117 against p. 125. Print neither until checked on a scan.
Do not present the Archidoxis magica as Paracelsus' own. Do not call it 'spurious by common consent' without a source either: the reports of Schneider (1982) disagree on whether parts are genuine.

Do not place it among Agrippa's alphabets. De occulta philosophia III.29–30 prints the Honorius letters, the Celestial, Malachim and 'passing through the River' (verified in the 1651 English, pp. 437–441), and the word 'Magi' does not occur in that text.
LETTER FORMS ARE NOT DESCRIBED. Drawing the alphabet from this file would mean inventing it. Trace from the 1539 print, and name the copy, because some of its alphabets were inked in by hand.
The Latin values are modern conventions. The transliterator may use them only if they are labelled as the site's convention, not as the alphabet's own.
No quotation is given. Fry's sentence is known only through Wikipedia's transcription and is given as a paraphrase. Omniglot's wording is seen, but Omniglot may not be used for history.
The ring-engraving story and Christian-style name-divination have no source and were removed.
